title_eng: Feasibility Test of Strip-type Unconstrained Sleep Monitoring System with Polysomnography
title_kor: Feasibility Test of Strip-type Unconstrained Sleep Monitoring System with Polysomnography
abstract:
Abstract— In this study, we used the commercialized strip - 
type sleep monitoring device and polysomnography 
simultaneously to measure the physiological signal during sleep 
and evaluated the feasibility of strip-type measurement system 
as a sleep monitoring technology. The results of the experiment 
conducted with 34 subjects showed that there was no significant 
difference between the two measurement in the mean heart rate 
during sleep (P>0.05), but there was a significant difference in 
the total sleep time (P<0.05), sleep efficiency (P<0.05), and 
average respiration rate (P<0.05) during sleep. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
In these days, there has been an increasing interest in 
digital healthcare, and devices that monitor sleep status by 
measuring physiological signals during sleep [1]. Particularly, 
many unconstrained signal measurement methods like strip of 
mat-type devices that can measure physiological signals 
without wearing the sensor directly have been introduced. The 
purpose of this study is to evaluate the feasibility of sle ep 
monitoring using a strip-type sensor. For this, we compare the 
results of the polysomnography (PSG) test with the 
commercialized strip-type sleep monitoring device and 
evaluate the unrestrained sleep monitoring performance of the 
strip-type sensor.

mat-type devices that can measure physiological signals

monitoring using a strip-type sensor. For this, we compare the 
results of the polysomnography (PSG) test with the 
commercialized strip-type sleep monitoring device and 
evaluate the unrestrained sleep monitoring performance of the

II. MATERIALS AND METHODS 
Beddit 2.0 Smart Sleep Tracker (Beddit, Espoo, Finland) 
was used as a strip type sleep monitoring device. We installed 
Beddit 2.0 under the bed cover, in the subject's chest location, 
and measured the signal simultaneously during the PSG 
experiment according to the instructions for use. We used 
Embla® N7000 (Natus Medical Inc., CA, USA) for PSG 
measurement. Total sleep time (minute), sleep efficiency (%), 
average heart rate (beat / minute) and average respiration rate 
(beat / minute) were collected from the measurement results of

Thirty-four subjects (31 male, 3 female) participated in the 
experiment. The age of the subjects was 44.5 ± 13.24 years and 
the BMI was 28.0 ± 4.5 kg/m2. According to the Apnea-
Hyponea Index (AHI) [2], 7 subjects have mild sleep apnea, 5 
have moderate sleep apnea, 17 have severe sleep apnea, and 5 
have no apnea. 
As a result, the total sleep time and the sleep efficiency 
measured from Beddit and PSG were confirmed in all subjects 
(N=34), but in Beddit's heart rate measurement results, nine 
subjects’ result were not reported. Also, the results of the PSG 
were missing the results of the respiration rate measurement of 
9 subjects. As a result, sleeping time and sleep efficiency were 
obtained from 34 subjects, however, the mean heart rate and 
respiration rate during sleep were derived with 25 subjects. 
III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS 
According to the results shown in Table 1, there was no 
significant difference in heart rate between the two 
measurement systems (P>0.05), however, Beddit 
overestimates the heart rate compared with PSG. On the other 
hands, in total sleep time, sleep efficiency and respiratory rate 
measurement, significant different were not found (P<0.05). In 
the statistical validation, the Wilcoxon signed rank test was 
used because all parameters showed no normality. 
IV. CONCLUSION 
In this study, we evaluate the feasibility of strip-type sensor 
in sleep monitoring by comparing the commercialized strip 
type sleep monitoring device and PSG. As a result, Beddit 2.0 
showed a tendency to overestimate in measuring total sleep 
time, sleep efficiency, respiration rate and heart rate 
monitoring, however, there was no significant difference in the 
heart rate measurement. This study suggests the possibility of 
a strip-type sensor. However, more rigorous analysis is still 
needed to provide more accurate verification. 
REFERENCES 
[1] J. M. Kelly, R. E. Strecker, and M. T. Bianchi, “Recent Developments 
in Home Sleep-Monitoring Devices,” ISRN Neurology, vol. 2012, p. 
10, September, 2012. 
[2] W. R. Ruegland, P. D. Rochford, F. J. O’Donoghue, R. J. Pierce, P. 
Singh and A. T. Thornton, “The new AASM criteria for scoring 
hypopneas: impact on the apnea hypopnea index,” Sleep, 32 (2), pp. 
150–157, February, 2009.
